topic: Research: JetBrains April 2026: Which AI Coding Tools Do Developers Actually Use at Work?
keyword: which ai coding tools developers use

key_points: JetBrains-based analysis in the source shows ChatGPT as clear usage leader, with strong Copilot adoption and much lower usage for Gemini.
The same article highlights the common split between broad trial/adoption and satisfaction, with high trial continuation for Claude but much lower initial usage share.
It also reports broad AI policy adoption, with most companies allowing third-party AI tools and only a minority fully restricting them.
Stack Overflow respondents show high AI mainstreaming: ChatGPT 81.7% and GitHub Copilot 67.9% are the leading out-of-the-box assistants in agent-use contexts.
AI agent users report strong adoption in software engineering, but accuracy, security, and workflow friction remain major concern areas.
Usage behavior is mixed by impact: productivity gains are acknowledged in task execution, while team-level collaboration impact is weaker than individual efficiency.
Sonar’s 2026 State of Code survey found broad daily usage among AI users and a large share of AI-generated committed code, indicating critical dependence on AI output.
It documents a reliability gap: most users do not fully trust AI-generated code, while routine verification remains inconsistent.
Security/governance concerns are rising as many teams use personal AI accounts or face extra review burdens despite AI productivity.
GitHub reports 4.7M paid GitHub Copilot subscribers and 77K organizations adopting Copilot, indicating strong long-term commercial traction.
Copilot remains a dominant platform in the GitHub ecosystem with paid enterprise and organization penetration reflected in Copilot-by-the-numbers.
The numbers suggest pricing and packaging decisions can materially shift user behavior in paid AI coding tool tiers.
Recent reporting indicates many technical workers now default to AI in normal workflows and are reluctant to complete work without it.
Independent and cited sources in the piece point to maintenance and debugging overhead as a counterweight to raw coding speed gains.
The article frames cost discipline as a major organizational constraint as teams balance adoption speed against AI-assisted technical debt.

stats.fact: JetBrains AI Pulse January 2026 found 90% of developers regularly use at least one AI tool for coding and development at work; 74% use specialized AI coding tools.

In the same JetBrains survey, GitHub Copilot remains the most known AI coding tool (76% awareness) with 29% work usage; Copilot growth is flattening, while Claude Code and Cursor are both at 18% adoption.
Stack Overflow’s 2025 AI dataset shows ChatGPT 81.7% and GitHub Copilot 67.9% as top out-of-the-box AI tools used by developers.
Sonar’s 2026 survey reports AI accounts for 42% of committed code today and is expected to rise to 65% by 2027; 96% of developers do not fully trust AI-generated code while only 48% always verify it.
GitHub’s newsroom page lists 4.7M paid Copilot subscribers and 77K organizations with Copilot adoption, reinforcing sustained platform-level demand.
Public commentary around the same period notes ongoing friction between speed gains and cost/governance: tokenized billing changes and hidden-cap style guardrails are driving tool-selection scrutiny.

angles: Mainstream adoption is no longer about whether AI is used, but about which model/tool mix produces fewer costly failures at scale.
Tool leadership is fragmenting between platform trust (Copilot distribution) and product fit/satisfaction (Claude Code, Cursor, specialized agents).
Verification, review overhead, and policy control are becoming the true production bottleneck rather than raw code-writing speed.
Enterprise tool selection is increasingly influenced by pricing architecture (usage tiers, caps, and token economics), not just feature marketing.
Teams that combine strong tooling with guardrails are likely to outperform those that treat AI as a replacement for architecture and QA discipline.
